paragraphs.source_en: Also the neighbouring shelter of Tin Torha, since the beginning of the 10th millennium, displays a certain degree of sedentism, indicated by the architectural arrangements of the site: stone semi-circles aligned against the back wall of the shelter were probably foundations of huts for family units and hearths, charcoal and the refuse of everyday life were also found. Barich (1998a) speaks about a true proto-village which fits in with the logistic mobility of complex hunter-gatherers who are using their territory with seasonal strategies. Similar stone structures were also found in the neighbouring shelter of Tin Torha Two Caves and in the Tassilian shelter of Tin Hanakaten (Aumassip 1980-1) and confirm the incipient sedentism which occurred in the Early Holocene, resulting from a prolonged exploitation of only one catchment area (Barich 1998a).

paragraphs.source_en: The faunal assemblage is composed of only wild animals; Barbary sheep (Ammotragus lervia) are the most exploited mammal in all excavated sites, and are represented by 80-70%. Percentages of fish and birds are also high, indicating an economy based on hunting and fishing. There is very rare evidence of pottery in this level and grinding equipment are also very rare, which may be related to a marginal emphasis on plant exploitation (Di Lerina 1999).

paragraphs.source_en: Conversely, the successive Mesolithic phase, dated between 8,900 and 8,000 BP, is characterised by a high incidence of grinding equipment and a macrolithic industry of low quality material, mainly on sandstone flakes. High quality materials diminish, with a low incidence of quartzite, while quartz and flint practically disappear. Good quality pottery is present. This phase features a broad spectrum of wild animal resources; several species are attested, small and big mammals, fish and birds. The remains of baskets containing the seeds of wild plants and a cord at Uan Afuda were dated between circa 8,300 and 8,700 BP. The site was probably inhabited for extended periods during the year, as the archaeological remains (grinding equipment, stone slabs and pottery) and settlement pattern seem to show.
